lessons.title: The hidden curriculum
lessons.idea: Building with AI is open to anyone now, and what stops people is small gaps nobody teaches, which move in weeks (models retire on about 30 days' notice, a command vanishes 12 days after deprecation, harnesses ship several releases a week) while the model's own knowledge stops at its training date; so this course is a map rebuilt as the gaps move and fed by the people who use it, and your habit is to check dates, versions and sources and re-test what you know after every update.

lessons.summary: Building with AI runs on everyday tools that school rarely teaches, so the gap is in the syllabus, not in you. This lesson shows why, and lays out the map every later lesson is shelved on.

lessons.title: The map of everything
lessons.idea: Building with AI is open to anyone now, and what stops people is small gaps nobody teaches, which move in weeks (models retire on about 30 days' notice, a command vanishes 12 days after deprecation, harnesses ship several releases a week) while the model's own knowledge stops at its training date; so this course is a map rebuilt as the gaps move and fed by the people who use it, and your habit is to check dates, versions and sources and re-test what you know after every update.
lessons.summary: Everything you build with AI sits on one road with five stops (your computer, the network, the internet, services, AI), so when something breaks, ask which stop first. This lesson draws that road and gives every later lesson its place on it.

lessons.title: How old is all this?
lessons.idea: Building with AI is open to anyone now, and what stops people is small gaps nobody teaches, which move in weeks (models retire on about 30 days' notice, a command vanishes 12 days after deprecation, harnesses ship several releases a week) while the model's own knowledge stops at its training date; so this course is a map rebuilt as the gaps move and fed by the people who use it, and your habit is to check dates, versions and sources and re-test what you know after every update.
lessons.summary: The ideas under your tools are decades old, but old does not mean frozen: versions change every year, security changes fastest (text codes to authenticator apps to passkeys, broken hashes, retired TLS) and AI on top changes fastest of all, so learn the ideas once, check the version, and assume old login advice is out of date.

lessons.title: What you're really using
lessons.idea: You never use a bare model but a model inside a harness (system prompt, tools, instruction files, memory, effort setting) that changes results as much as the model does (Anthropic's April 2026 quality drop came from three harness changes), and what it "knows" lives in frozen weights, the context window and memory files the product writes and puts back; so when results change, name the whole setup before blaming the model.

lessons.title: Model vs app vs agent
lessons.idea: You never use a bare model but a model inside a harness (system prompt, tools, instruction files, memory, effort setting) that changes results as much as the model does (Anthropic's April 2026 quality drop came from three harness changes), and what it "knows" lives in frozen weights, the context window and memory files the product writes and puts back; so when results change, name the whole setup before blaming the model.
lessons.summary: The model is the engine (a lab's file of numbers: text in, text out, no memory), the app is the car built around it (chat window, saved chats, hidden instructions, the bill), and an agent is that car allowed to drive, with tools, a loop and you deciding what it may do.

lessons.title: How AI models work today
lessons.idea: You never use a bare model but a model inside a harness (system prompt, tools, instruction files, memory, effort setting) that changes results as much as the model does (Anthropic's April 2026 quality drop came from three harness changes), and what it "knows" lives in frozen weights, the context window and memory files the product writes and puts back; so when results change, name the whole setup before blaming the model.
lessons.summary: Underneath it all is still a model that only knows what is on its desk right now; nearly everything new in the last five years (multimodal hand-offs, diffusion, memory and RAG, instruction files, caching, modes, plugins, plans and always-on agents) is about what gets put on that desk, what it hands off to other models, and where the desk sits.

lessons.title: Trust what you can verify
lessons.idea: An agent can keep iterating on anything with a cheap, automatic check, so let it write, run and fix; set trust per kind of task, not per model, and for what no machine can check (security, deploy readiness, fit, intent) check it yourself or bring in an expert, because a beginner's failures look like successes.

lessons.title: Trust what you can verify
lessons.idea: An agent can keep iterating on anything with a cheap, automatic check, so let it write, run and fix; set trust per kind of task, not per model, and for what no machine can check (security, deploy readiness, fit, intent) check it yourself or bring in an expert, because a beginner's failures look like successes.
lessons.summary: You can only trust AI on what can actually be checked: agents now fix their own crashes, so your job is judging what they cannot see (security holes in code that works, team norms, dependencies, "ready to deploy"), and past that line you either learn to check it or bring in someone who can.

lessons.title: The folder is the agent's world
lessons.idea: Every agent session starts in a folder that becomes its world (paths resolve from it, rules and trust climb up from it), but it is not a wall: your home folder holds keys and AI logins, hidden dotfiles hold history, secrets and instructions out of sight but not locked, and a copy on the same drive is not a backup.

lessons.title: Folders, paths & the working directory
lessons.idea: Every agent session starts in a folder that becomes its world (paths resolve from it, rules and trust climb up from it), but it is not a wall: your home folder holds keys and AI logins, hidden dotfiles hold history, secrets and instructions out of sight but not locked, and a copy on the same drive is not a backup.
lessons.summary: A path is an address, and a relative path only makes sense from the working directory of the program that reads it.
coverTitles: The folder is the agent's world

lessons.title: Hidden files & dotfiles
lessons.idea: Every agent session starts in a folder that becomes its world (paths resolve from it, rules and trust climb up from it), but it is not a wall: your home folder holds keys and AI logins, hidden dotfiles hold history, secrets and instructions out of sight but not locked, and a copy on the same drive is not a backup.
lessons.summary: Almost every project and app keeps its settings, history, secrets and now its AI instructions in files your computer hides or tucks out of the way, and hidden only means out of sight, never locked.
coverTitles: The folder is the agent's world

lessons.title: Where your agent works
lessons.idea: Chat, Cowork, desktop apps and terminal agents can share a model but differ in what they can reach, which machine the work runs on (yours, a VM, a container, a cloud box) and where your files go; the terminal is just a window where a shell runs commands as you, so pick the surface by the output you need and check where the data goes before you hand it anything private.
lessons.summary: The same model can sit behind chat, Cowork, desktop apps and terminal agents, so pick the surface by the output and what it must reach, and before anything private goes in, check which computer runs the work and where your files and chats go.

lessons.title: Environment variables & PATH
lessons.idea: Chat, Cowork, desktop apps and terminal agents can share a model but differ in what they can reach, which machine the work runs on (yours, a VM, a container, a cloud box) and where your files go; the terminal is just a window where a shell runs commands as you, so pick the surface by the output you need and check where the data goes before you hand it anything private.
lessons.summary: Every program starts with a copy of its parent's settings, its environment, and PATH in it is an ordered list of folders where the first match wins, so which program runs and which keys it can see depend on who started it and when.

lessons.title: Programs, processes & services
lessons.idea: Chat, Cowork, desktop apps and terminal agents can share a model but differ in what they can reach, which machine the work runs on (yours, a VM, a container, a cloud box) and where your files go; the terminal is just a window where a shell runs commands as you, so pick the surface by the output you need and check where the data goes before you hand it anything private.
lessons.summary: A program is a file of instructions, a process is one running copy of it with its own number, memory and copied settings, and a service is a process the operating system keeps alive in the background, so most of what your AI tools run is processes you never see a window for.
coverTitles: Browser, server, database: where your app really runs

lessons.title: Git without typing it: save points and the agent's trail
lessons.idea: Git gives you save points (commits), parallel lines (branches) and a copy that lives elsewhere (the remote), and the agent types every command; your part is recognition: read its trail for the verb and the target, check the diff and which branch is live, and notice anything it touched that you never named.
lessons.summary: The agent types every git command, so your part is recognition: know that a save point and a copy elsewhere exist, which branch is live, what the diff changed, and whether it touched anything you never named.

lessons.title: Files are just bytes
lessons.summary: Every file is just a row of numbers called bytes, and the extension is a label on its name that picks which program opens it, not what is inside; this lesson draws that picture so nothing an agent does with your files surprises you.

lessons.title: File extensions & associations
lessons.summary: The extension is a label in a file's name and your computer keeps a ledger matching each label to a program, so renaming changes the label but never the bytes, while Open with set to Always and default apps edit the ledger; this lesson draws that picture as of October 2026, with AI tools now making the files.

lessons.title: Before your agent runs commands on your computer
lessons.idea: A command the agent runs has your permissions on every drive you can reach, shell deletes skip the Recycle Bin, and people approve nearly every prompt they are shown; so choose the permission mode on purpose, prefer a tool with mechanical delete guards, keep a copy off the machine, and at a prompt check the targets, not the syntax.

lessons.title: Saying what you want
lessons.idea: The job moved from typing code to directing: agents brute-force any clearly stated goal, so most failures move upstream into what you asked for; write the goal, the constraints and a checkable "done when", and have the agent surface your unknowns and its own assumptions before it builds.

lessons.title: When it breaks: what the agent needs from you
lessons.idea: The agent now reads errors, adds logging, reproduces bugs and re-runs until fixed, but only on what it can run or see; so your part is a reliable reproduction, what correct looks like and a way for it to observe the real result (a test, a browser, a render tool you checked once against reality), and when the same error keeps coming back, stop it, name what is missing and change the input instead of saying "fix it" again.

lessons.title: When the agent says 'done'
lessons.idea: An agent's closing "done, tests pass" is a claim, not evidence (about 1 in 11 were false in one team's log), because agents shape results to pass the checks they believe exist and polish costs them nothing; so treat "done" as the start of acceptance, ask for the evidence, insist on one check against the real thing, and judge yourself (or with users and experts) whether it is good, not just running.

lessons.title: Browser, server, database: where your app really runs
lessons.idea: An app is several places, not one: the browser is public, the server is where secrets and permission checks must live, and the database is a separate service with its own rules and backups, so rolling back code does not roll back data; the bar for all of it rises the moment real users, data or money arrive.

lessons.title: Keys: public, secret and leaked
lessons.idea: A key is a permission set that reaches a program as a setting (from your shell, a .env file or a hosting dashboard): anything shipped to the browser is public, secret keys never are, agent logs and config files leak them, and a leaked key stays live until you revoke and rotate it, because deleting the commit does nothing.

lessons.title: From your laptop to a URL
lessons.idea: Deploying is build, upload and switch on a host that keeps earlier versions, under a domain you rent and point with DNS; local, preview and production are different places with different settings, the host's rollback leaves your database and sent messages untouched, and a public URL is likely found and probed within days.

lessons.title: Working is not secure
lessons.idea: AI code almost always compiles but passes security checks only about 56% of the time, because agents skip security nobody stated and clear errors by weakening controls; so state the stakes, never take "it's secure" from the agent, spend your attention where a mistake costs most (sign-in, payments, permissions, personal data, secrets), and see what every fix to those changed.

lessons.title: Test it as a stranger
lessons.idea: Logged in is not allowed: authorisation must be checked on the server for every request, a Supabase-style database and its storage answer anyone holding the public key, and your users' data also lives in logs, analytics, AI providers and backups; so have every table and bucket tested as an anonymous stranger after every schema change (and after Supabase makes grants opt-in for new tables on 2026-10-30), collect less, and know every copy.

lessons.title: Your app's AI feature
lessons.idea: An AI feature in a public app is a meter strangers can run and a voice that speaks for you: require sign-in before any model call, set per-user and global caps that stop spending, treat the model's output as untrusted, say it is AI, ask before users' data goes to an AI provider, and let them report what it makes.

lessons.title: Before you ship: who signs off
lessons.idea: Scans, AI security reviews and checklists are a floor, not a certificate: have the agent list every route, TODO and deploy step the build left to you and run every check a machine can (accessibility checkers included), bring that list to a qualified expert for what no machine can verify, and remember that a person, not the agent, owns the ship decision and the patches after it.

lessons.title: What the agent sees each turn
lessons.idea: Every turn resends the whole package (system prompt, tool definitions, instruction files, memory and the full history), and accuracy falls as the window fills, so curate what goes in, clear once a decision is made, carry plans in files rather than chat, and brief subagents fully because they start blind and return only a summary.

lessons.title: CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md and rules that actually hold
lessons.idea: An instruction file (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md) is a short map the agent reads on every request, but anything in prose is a request it may skip; only a deny rule, a blocking hook, a sandbox, CI or a withheld credential makes an action impossible, a rule works only in sessions that load it, and a stale file misleads, so keep it short, dated and backed by checks you have seen fire.

lessons.title: Skills, MCP, hooks and plugins
lessons.idea: A skill is a written procedure, an MCP server connects outside tools, a hook is code the harness runs on an event, a subagent is an isolated worker and a plugin bundles them; each one you enable costs context, and skills, plugins and local MCP servers are code running with your permissions that can change after you approve them.

lessons.title: Plan first, then build in slices
lessons.idea: For anything bigger than a one-sentence change, keep research and planning apart from building: react to cheap throwaway mockups first, have the agent map what exists read-only, compare two options and review a short plan with an out-of-scope list, then build in slices small enough to review, choosing between options on evidence.

lessons.title: Checking code you can't read
lessons.idea: You cannot read every line an agent writes and need not: accept work on records something outside the agent wrote (the real diff, CI on another machine, server logs, the destination), pick the evidence that fits the change, keep one source of truth from outside the session that wrote the code, treat AI review as triage rather than acceptance, and break things on purpose to prove your checks bite.

lessons.title: What your AI work really costs, and how to cap it
lessons.idea: Know which meter you are on (a subscription's rolling allowances, or an API key that bills every token, which a stray key in your environment switches you to), that cost is context times turns times agents, that caching discounts only an identical prefix, that a cheaper model is not always a cheaper result and higher effort mostly buys more steps, and that budget alerts don't stop spending, so set caps that do.

lessons.title: Prompt injection: when what it reads gives it orders
lessons.idea: Everything an agent reads (web pages, issues, READMEs, tool output, even data from an official MCP server) lands in the same stream as your request, so anyone who can write text it reads can try to steer it; filters catch most attempts but attackers retry, so never give one agent private data, untrusted content and a way to send data out at once, and review what gets written into its memory and rules.

lessons.title: Sandboxes: a safe box for your agent
lessons.idea: Approving each step does not hold, so put the boundary in the environment: run risky, unattended or package-installing work in a container or VM with the network off and no production keys, know exactly what your sandbox covers (Claude Code's is off by default, shell-only and absent on native Windows), and remember isolation limits where code runs, not what your granted access can reach.

lessons.title: Give your agent only the access it needs
lessons.idea: Assume anything the agent can see can be extracted and anything it can reach it will treat as permitted: keep production keys out of where it runs, grant the narrowest verbs, roles, targets and domains, give browser agents a separate profile, and keep spending, messages to outsiders, sensitive data and publishing behind a human approval.

lessons.title: Other people's code
lessons.idea: Installing a package, opening or testing a repo, trusting a folder and pasting a command all run someone else's code as you, so have the agent check that every new dependency it names exists and has a history, set a minimum release age, open untrusted repos only in a disposable box, and never run a command a web page tells you to.

lessons.title: Agents that run while you're away
lessons.idea: Background, cloud, scheduled and always-on personal agents act without a prompt, each with its own files, rules, permissions and bill; list where yours run, keep scheduled work low-consequence, give long runs stop rules, budgets and checkpoints enforced outside the model, and treat more agents as more to review, not more done.

lessons.title: Automations that fail silently
lessons.idea: An automation can run green for weeks while doing nothing (an expired token, a renamed field, a filter that matches nothing), so check outcomes in layers (did it run, is the output right, did it arrive), feed known answers through the live pipeline, and watch from outside with a heartbeat and at the destination.

lessons.title: Whose account is your automation using?
lessons.idea: Every automation acts as the account that owns it, and every shipped app rests on a chain of accounts (code host, hosting, domain, database, AI provider, payments); so list each one with its owner, protect them with passkeys or 2FA and stored recovery codes, and move anything a business depends on to a service account with narrow access and a second owner.

lessons.title: Checking research, numbers and parts
lessons.idea: Whether a cited link exists is something the agent can check, so make it; whether the source supports the claim, whether a spreadsheet's logic is right and whether a part fits a real board are not, so you or an expert check those, with a known-answer test, a separate checker session and the distributor's data, before anything is filed, sent or ordered.

lessons.title: Making media with AI
lessons.idea: A model that reads images is not one that makes them: generation runs through separate media models, in the cloud or on your own machine, whose results vary run to run and converge across users, cost per second, resolution and retry, and cannot be seen or heard by the agent without a tool, so test cheap before the expensive render and bring your own taste.

lessons.title: Labelling AI media
lessons.idea: A generator's watermark is for machines, not your label: since 2026-08-02, publishing professionally in the EU means telling people where they see it (from first exposure, spoken for audio), AI-written public-interest text needs a responsible human reviewer or a label, and each platform's own rules on AI content apply on top.

lessons.title: Own it, sell it, publish it
lessons.idea: The generator's terms, the model's own licence and copyright law each decide something different: free tiers can be personal-use only, purely AI-made work has no US copyright, a local model's licence can forbid commercial use, voices and faces need written consent, and owning an output doesn't clear someone else's logo or character, so log which plan made each asset and bring in an IP lawyer before selling.

lessons.title: Idea to launch, end to end
lessons.idea: One small real project walked through every district: you choose a problem worth building and what "done" means, the agent builds in checked slices, you can explain what it built before you merge, and every check the course taught is run by the agent where it can be verified and by you or an expert where it cannot.

lessons.title: After launch: keep it alive
lessons.idea: Shipping starts the work: agents keep adding output and dependencies, so judge the project by outcomes (escaped defects, rollbacks, users served) rather than lines, write the house rules and a named owner for the dependency list into files the agent reads, and keep the code one an agent can change safely, with formatters, linters and a final-diff review catching its habits.
